name: Tangerine
lede: Tangerine is the strong orange of the fruit's skin, a color that is rare as a large area in old paintings but turns up as the spark in many.

sections.title: The fruit's orange
sections.body:
Saint Clair's glossary describes tangerine simply as a yellowy orange, named from the skin of the fruit [1]. Paterson lists it in his table of orange names, and Maerz and Paul recorded it in 1930, giving 1899 for the first use of the color name in their sources [2][3]. The books read say nothing further on where the name began.

The swatch matches the ISCC-NBS block for a strong orange almost exactly, about 2.4 units away [3]. The xkcd survey of 2010 gives a slightly brighter orange for the same word [3]. Close neighbors are [[orange]], [[mandarin]] and [[persian-orange]].

sections.title: A color that vibrates
sections.body: Livingstone, a vision scientist, quotes David Sedaris on a house painted hot pink with tangerine trim, whose doors and windows seemed to tremble [4]. She uses it to illustrate equiluminant colors, hues of similar brightness that can seem to jitter when placed together [4]. In the Netherlands, many people dress in luminous tangerine for the King's Day holiday each April [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch appears in 29 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.12 per cent, in at least five per cent of the canvas [5]. In 94 per cent of the 36 paintings where the within-painting search finds it, it is an accent, not a ground [5]. It peaks in the 1800s, 24 paintings, at 1.8 times the expected rate [5]. The widest example is an 1830 Kota painting from India, where it covers about 31 per cent [5]. Bonnard's [[painting:commons-Q17491092|Corner of a table]] of 1935 and Gauguin's [[painting:commons-Q17493569|Les Alyscamps]] of 1888 also carry it [5]. This is photographed color from aged, varnished surfaces, not a pigment test [5].
